::: {.why}
Every backtest you have run this year computes positions as an array operation, which is fast and which quietly assumes several things you listed last night.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Name three things a vectorised backtest cannot represent and one thing it gets right that an event-driven engine often gets wrong.
- Give two reasons the two architectures legitimately disagree and one that means you have a bug.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Write the comparison out: a vectorised backtest cannot represent partial fills, order rejection, intraday sequencing, position-dependent sizing, or a stop that triggers within a bar. An event-driven engine represents all of those and is slower by two orders of magnitude, which changes what research you can afford to do.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the source of a small event-driven engine, backtesting.py, specifically its main loop and its order handling. It is a few hundred readable lines and reading it is faster than reading the documentation.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Decide and record the architecture you will build: an event loop over sessions rather than over ticks, which keeps the sequencing honest without paying for intraday simulation you have no data for.
:::
:::
